title: What makes the Sun shine?
new_ideas: device CoalSun — the Sun gripped in giant iron tongs like a lump of coal, burning down to cinders

lines.text: Some physicists blamed Davis’s tank. Others blamed the theory of the Sun. Davis just kept counting, and his number would not *budge*.

acts: the camera travels on toward the counter

lines.text: For thirty years nobody could say. The prediction hung on the wall while posters changed, and hair turned *grey*.

lines.text: The answer came from another mine, in Canada. Deep underground, a giant ball of heavy water, watched by thousands of electric *eyes*.

plan.see: The wall cracks open into a vast cavern; a giant sphere stands in it, studded with thousands of light sensors.

lines.text: It could catch neutrinos of every kind. And it turns out there are three kinds, like three different *flavours*.

lines.text: And on the long flight from the Sun, a neutrino can change from one kind into *another*.

plan.see: A neutrino in a red coat walks in at one door and steps out of another in a blue coat.

lines.text: Davis’s tank could only see one kind. The missing two thirds had never been missing at all. They had changed their *coats*.

lines.text: In 2001 and 2002, Sudbury counted all three kinds together. Would the total match the prediction? It did. The Sun really is a nuclear *furnace*.

lines.text: Ray Davis won a Nobel Prize in 2002. The neutrino hunters behind the final answer won one in *2015*.

lines.text: So here is what the Sun really is. Every second, it turns about four million tonnes of itself into *light*.

lines.text: It has been doing that for four and a half billion years, and it has billions of years still to *go*.
